strengths: Provides a clean, intuitive, and mathematically sound analysis explaining why fine-tuning the value bias (b_v) is superior to query (b_q) and key (b_k) biases, utilizing softmax properties and attention weight sparsity.

Presents an extensive and rigorous empirical evaluation spanning encoder-only and decoder-only architectures (up to 6.7B parameters), including masked models (BERT, RoBERTa) and autoregressive models (OPT, LLaMA-2).

Cleverly extends the findings to modern 'bias-free' LLMs (such as LLaMA-2, DeepSeek-Coder, and GPT-J) by manually injecting bias terms, showing that the key finding still holds and offers exceptional parameter efficiency.
Demonstrates compatibility and synergy with popular PEFT frameworks (LoRA, VeRA, DoRA, PiSSA), supported by thorough statistical significance testing (paired t-tests).
weaknesses: The proposed metric combining magnitude and angular changes serves primarily as an analytical tool rather than an active selection algorithm, as the final practical recommendation is simply to always fine-tune b_v in low-data regimes.
While the analysis of individual bias terms is highly detailed, the practical execution of training only a subset of biases represents a relatively incremental variant of BitFit.

strengths: The paper presents an elegant and theoretically sound explanation of why fine-tuning the value bias ($b_v$) is highly expressive compared to the query ($b_q$) and key ($b_k$) biases, utilizing the properties of softmax shift-invariance and attention matrix sparsity.

The proposed method of combining magnitude changes with angular changes (vector projections) offers a much more accurate and dynamic way to select target bias terms compared to traditional pure magnitude-based or Fisher-based approaches.

The empirical validation is exceptionally thorough, spanning encoder-only models (BERT, RoBERTa) and decoder-only autoregressive models (OPT, LLaMA-2) up to 6.7B parameters, and showcasing consistency across several classification, multiple-choice, and generation datasets.

The approach is shown to be highly practical; it easily generalizes to bias-free LLMs (such as LLaMA-2 and GPT-J) through manual injection and seamlessly integrates with mainstream PEFT methods like LoRA, VeRA, and DoRA.
weaknesses: The performance advantage of fine-tuning $b_v$ alone (relative to $b_q$ or full-parameter tuning) is primarily pronounced in low-data regimes, with the performance gap showing a narrowing trend as the training data scale increases to high-data regimes.

The analysis is heavily concentrated on standard dot-product attention projection biases, while leaving the investigation of other potential bias terms (such as LayerNorm and feed-forward network biases) largely out of scope.

strengths: Provides an exceptionally elegant and clear mathematical analysis explaining why the value bias ($b_v$) is highly expressive compared to query ($b_q$) and key ($b_k$) biases. The proof that $b_k$ has zero effect on attention weights due to softmax shift-invariance, while $b_v$ adds full-dimensional linear freedom to the output space, is highly insightful.

Proposes an incredibly simple and ultra-parameter-efficient method (BEFT) that requires as little as 0.01% of parameters, yielding competitive performance in low-data regimes without any extra structural overhead or auxiliary configurations.

Presents a very thorough and comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple model architectures (encoder-only, decoder-only, and bias-free models like LLaMA-2) and diverse tasks (classification, multiple-choice, and generation).

Successfully reconciles prior literature's claims regarding bias magnitude changes by incorporating angular dynamics, demonstrating that direction matters as much as magnitude when mapping weight dynamics to downstream task performance.
weaknesses: The evaluation is primarily focused on and optimized for low-data regimes; the relative performance benefits of fine-tuning only the $b_v$ terms may diminish or saturate when large-scale training data is available.

While the paper is generally very well-written, the transition between the angular change metric definition in Section 2 and the expressiveness proofs could be structured a bit more tightly to improve narrative flow.
